A Year 5 history gallery

Before the Gold

Eight pictures of Sydney, all painted or printed before anyone found gold. Nobody in them knows what is about to happen to their town.

So your work can be printed at the end.
Station 00

Hold onto this number

Before you look at a single picture, you need to know how many people were living here.
36,598People in the whole colony of New South Wales, 1828 census
10,815People in Sydney town itself, 1828 census

Ten thousand people in the town. That is about fifteen large primary schools, spread across the whole of Sydney.

Everything you are about to look at was built by, and for, roughly that many people.

Keep the number in your head. At the very last station you will be asked to guess what happened to it.
Station 00

Before you look

Two things to read, then the gallery opens.
A note before you look These pictures were made on the lands of the Gadigal people of the Eora Nation, who had lived here for tens of thousands of years before 1788. Some of the paintings show Aboriginal people, and this gallery includes information about what happened to those communities. Take care with it, and be respectful in what you write.
How this gallery works Seventeen pages. Use the arrows at the bottom, or the left and right keys on your keyboard. Every picture can be zoomed, dragged and magnified. One station will not open until you have written down what you notice, because noticing comes first and being told comes second. Nothing here is marked right or wrong.
Station 01

Look before you are told

This painting has ten things labelled on it. You cannot see the labels yet. Zoom in, drag around, use the magnifier, and write three things of your own first.
Drag to move. Scroll to zoom. Double click to zoom to a spot.
Sydney Cove, unidentified artist, about the 1820s. Watercolour. State Library of New South Wales
Notice one
One thing you can see that you did not expect.
Notice two
One thing that is missing, compared with a town today.
Notice three
One question you would ask the person who painted this.
Write something in all three boxes first.
Station 02

I spy, 1827

Ten years later, a different painter, a much finer brush. Click on the picture where you think each thing is. No labels, no arrows. You have to actually find it.
Click the picture to place your guess.
Sydney from the North Shore, attributed to Joseph Lycett, 1827. Watercolour. Dixson Galleries, State Library of New South Wales
Find these ten things

Click one to make it the target, then click on the painting where you think it is.

Pick something to hunt for. 0 / 10
Joseph Lycett was a convict. He was transported to New South Wales for forgery, which means faking documents and money. In the colony he was put to work painting careful, flattering views of the settlement that were sent back to England for people to admire. Hold that thought while you hunt.
Station 03

Read a building

A colony shows what it cares about by what it spends its stone on. Drag each description onto the right part of the picture.
Tap a card, then tap the picture.
Convict Barrack, Sydney, N.S. Wales, unidentified artist, about 1820. Watercolour. Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales
Five descriptions

Every one of these is true. Work out which part of the picture it belongs to.

Five to place.
Then think
The colony built this before it built a hospital big enough for everyone, and before it had running water. What does that tell you about what the people in charge were most worried about?
The barracks. It opened on 4 June 1819 and 589 convict men were admitted on the first day. It was built for 600. By 1840 a convict called Charles Cozens counted about 1,300 men sleeping there in hammocks. Later the same building held newly arrived single women, then orphans.
Station 03

A church and a courthouse

The second building the colony chose to spend its stone on. Zoom right in on the printed words at the bottom.
There is a library stamp under the caption. Find it.
St James’ Church, Supreme Court House &c., John Gardiner Austin, 1836. Hand coloured lithograph. Dixson Library, State Library of New South Wales
One question
A church and a courthouse, standing side by side, and the convict barracks is just out of frame to the right. All three were designed by the same man. Why would a government put those three buildings together in one place?
Look closer
Two men on horseback are in the middle of the road, and two people on foot are behind a fence. What is the painter telling you by putting them where he has?
No taps. Sydney had no running water. The Tank Stream was abandoned in 1826 because tanneries and slaughterhouses had polluted it. Convict gangs then dug Busby’s Bore, a 3.6 kilometre tunnel, mostly by pick through rock, working in three eight hour shifts around the clock from 1827 to 1837. Water was then sold from the end of the tunnel into carts.
Station 03

A castle for horses

The third building. A pencil drawing rather than a painting, which means you are seeing the artist think.
Find the person, the cattle and the pencilled date.
Sydney, Government House Stables from the Domain, Charles Rodius, 1830. Pencil. State Library of New South Wales
One question
This castle, with turrets and a gateway, was built to house the Governor’s horses. Convicts built it. What is the message a building like this sends to the people who walk past it every day?

The building is still standing. It is now the Sydney Conservatorium of Music.

Three buildings, one message
A barracks, a courthouse and a stable. If those are the three grandest buildings in your town, what kind of place are you living in?
Getting here. A sailing voyage from England took roughly 70 to 110 days. Today the flight takes about 22 hours. If you were sent here as a convict there was no way of going back, and no way of sending a quick message home.

Twelve statements about what these paintings show. The third pile matters most. A painting can only tell you some things, and a good historian knows the difference.
The cards

Signs it is still small

Evidence that this is a town, not a city.

Signs it is growing

Evidence that money, people and ambition are arriving.

You cannot tell from a picture

True or not, a painting is the wrong place to look for it.

Tap a card, then tap a pile. Or drag it.

Ten years apart

Sydney in about 1817 on the left, the same harbour in 1827 in the middle. These are not the same viewpoint, so you cannot slide one over the other. You have to compare feature by feature.
Sydney Harbour, from Edward Charles Close, Sketchbook of New South Wales views, about 1817. Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales
“Sydney in all its Glory”, Edward Charles Close, about 1817. The title is written across the top in the artist’s own hand. Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales
Sydney from the North Shore, attributed to Joseph Lycett, 1827. Dixson Galleries, State Library of New South Wales
Change tally

Tick only what you can actually see evidence for.

Station 05

What would have changed

Roughly six thousand more people arrived in those ten years. Think about what that would have felt like from the inside.
The hard question
If you had grown up in Sydney between 1817 and 1827, what would have felt different about your everyday life?
Those windmills. They ground wheat into flour so the town could have bread. Hand mills could not keep up. By the 1820s windmills stood all the way from The Rocks to Parramatta, and Millers Point is named after them. Counting them is a rough measure of how many mouths there were to feed.
Still no railway, no bridge, no telegraph. The harbour was the road. If you wanted to cross it, you rowed. If you wanted news from England, you waited three or four months for a ship.
Station 05

Nine years later again

1836. Look along the skyline and see how much has filled in.
Use the magnifier on the far shore.
Sydney Cove from the North Shore, Conrad Martens, 1836. Watercolour. Dixson Galleries, State Library of New South Wales

Conrad Martens, 1836

He had sailed as ship’s artist on HMS Beagle and met Charles Darwin before he settled in Sydney. He scratched at the paper with a blade to make the white sparkle on the water.

By 1836 there were about 19,700 people in Sydney town and roughly 77,000 in the colony. Compare that with the 10,815 you were holding onto from 1828.

Notice
Martens has put a huge rock and some scrubby bush in the front, and pushed the town far away into the haze. Why might a painter make the bush big and the town small?
Station 06

Whose Sydney is this?

In two of these eight pictures, Aboriginal people stand closest to you, looking out at a town on their own Country. The painters chose to put them there.
Sydney Cove, about the 1820s, right foreground.
Sydney from the North Shore, 1827, foreground.
Respond on the line
“These paintings tell us the truth about what Sydney was really like.”
Station 06

Choosing a caption

Three captions for the 1827 painting. All three are true. Which one goes on the gallery wall?
Choose a caption
One sentence
Across all eight pictures, name a group of people who lived in Sydney but who you almost never see. Why might a painter leave them out?
What the records say

In January 1788 Governor Phillip counted about 1,500 Aboriginal people around Port Jackson, though historians think his count was far too low, because he only saw what was in front of him in one season.

The City of Sydney’s Aboriginal history project records that the Gadigal clan numbered around 60 people in 1788, and that by 1791, after the smallpox epidemic of 1789, only three were left.

Every one of the paintings in this gallery was made after that.

Station 07

Now watch it move

Someone has fed paintings like these into an artificial intelligence and asked it to make them move. It is beautiful. It is also not evidence.
If the video does not load, open it at youtube.com/watch?v=ZjZB6ZTc-_Q
Added, or invented?
Name one thing that moves in the video which nobody in the 1820s wrote down or painted. The AI made it up because it had to make something up.
Then judge it
Two things can both be true. What did the animation help you understand? What did it take away?
Why this matters. A painting is a source: a real person stood somewhere real and chose what to put in. An animation made from that painting is an interpretation of an interpretation. It can make the past feel closer. It cannot tell you anything new, because it has no extra information. It only has guesses that look convincing.
Station 08

What happens next

On 12 February 1851 gold was found at Lewis Ponds Creek near Bathurst. Within months there was gold in Victoria too. Drag the gold dot to where you think 1861 belongs.
Drag the gold dot up or down.

1,153,973

In 1851 there were about 403,889 non-Aboriginal people in the whole of Australia. Ten years later there were 1,153,973. Nearly three times as many, in ten years, because of gold.

They came from Britain, Ireland, Germany, the United States and, in very large numbers, from southern China. The colony you have been looking at, the one small enough to fit into a few watercolours, was gone.

Before you reveal it
Say why you put the dot where you did.

Where these pictures live. All eight are held by the State Library of New South Wales, in the Mitchell Library and Dixson collections. Population figures come from the 1861 New South Wales census tables and from T. A. Coghlan’s official statistics of the Australian colonies. Facts about the Hyde Park Barracks come from Museums of History NSW, and facts about Busby’s Bore and the windmills from the Dictionary of Sydney. Information about the Gadigal people comes from the City of Sydney’s Sydney Barani project and the Australian Museum.
